payload.problem_addressed: Existing KV-cache compression for LLM structured generation (JSON/SQL/function calls) discards the task-relevant structural signal already exposed by constrained-decoding parser transitions, forcing a choice between task accuracy and memory/latency savings.
payload.method_summary: PASK (Parser-Aware Structural KV Persistence) tags each generated token with a structural bucket derived from its constrained-decoding parser transition (class/role/state/next) crossed with a Transformer layer group, then offline-calibrates a persistence policy over {release, retain-low, retain-high} using task-error sensitivity (to set protection floors) and attention-output distortion (to allocate residual KV budget); at decode time it performs only a lightweight structure-conditioned table lookup, with no online importance estimation.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces PASK, an offline-calibrated, online-lookup KV persistence policy that reuses parser transitions already produced by grammar-constrained decoding to decide, per token and layer group, how much KV precision to retain. It shows that combining a task-error-sensitivity protection floor with a distortion-ranked residual budget preserves substantially more function-calling accuracy under aggressive KV compression than prior attention-based or structure-aware KV compression baselines, while also cutting peak GPU memory and improving serving throughput/latency.
key_architecture_choices: Structural buckets z_t = (class, role, state, next) derived purely from the constrained decoder's parser transition, not from attention statistics
Three discrete persistence actions (Release/Retain-Low/Retain-High) per layer group, calibrated offline into a frozen lookup table
Two-signal calibration: task-error sensitivity sets minimum protection floors; attention-output distortion ranks residual budget upgrades
Separate decode-side policy and a lightweight prefill-side 'companion' policy for prompt tokens
datasets: BFCL non-live and Live subsets (function-calling benchmark)
metrics: BFCL AST-checker accuracy (overall and per category)
payload.headline_results: On Qwen3-4B-Instruct at a total KV budget of ~0.33, PASK reaches 88.00% BFCL non-live accuracy (vs. 91.83% Full KV, 78.67% best other compressed baseline TriAxialKV), reduces peak GPU memory by ~47.5% vs Full KV, and cuts TPOT by up to 69.8% while raising throughput by up to ~99% at matched budget; trends hold at Qwen3-14B.
claimed_advantages: Reuses structure the constrained decoder already computes, adding no online importance-estimation cost
Consistently beats attention-based (H2O, SnapKV, RocketKV) and other structure-aware KV baselines (TriAxialKV, Transactional Attention) on accuracy at matched compression budget
Large accuracy gains concentrated on structurally hard categories (parallel/parallel-multiple function calls)
limitations: Requires a one-time offline calibration stage before deployment
Uses only three coarse layer groups and three discrete persistence actions; finer-grained partitioning is left to future work
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Not directly about program correctness, but the core idea — using the decoder's own grammar/parser state (which our closed-vocabulary DSL decoding already tracks) to identify which token positions are structurally/schema-critical — could inform where to spend extra decoding budget (e.g. beam width, verifier calls, or repair effort) in our hex-meshing DSL decoder: critical positions like block/sweep/projection command heads or coordinate-pointer tokens vs. low-risk filler tokens. Marginal relevance for our own KV/inference-efficiency concerns if the decoder is ever served at scale.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is primarily an inference-efficiency (KV cache compression) paper for existing LLM agents doing JSON/SQL/function-calling, evaluated only on BFCL with Qwen3 models; it does not address structural validity of the *generated* program itself (constrained decoding already guarantees that), only serving cost. Relevance to hexgen is via analogy (parser-state-conditioned resource allocation), not a directly transferable method.
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: L (requires an offline calibration pipeline over parser transitions and layer groups; not directly reusable without significant adaptation)
dependencies_on_other_methods: Constrained/grammar decoding backends (XGrammar, SGLang) that expose parser transitions

provenance.problem_addressed: Existing KV compression largely leaves this task-relevant structural signal unused.
provenance.method_summary: PASK ... turns parser-derived structure into layer-group-specific KV persistence decisions.
provenance.headline_results: At a targe total KV budget of 0.33, PASK outperforms the strongest compressed baseline by 17.39 percentage points on average
provenance.limitations: PASK requires an offline calibration stage to construct the structure-conditioned policy table, introducing a one-time preprocessing cost before deployment.

payload.problem_addressed: Grammar-constrained decoders that only enforce local prefix feasibility (each token keeps the prefix extendable to *some* valid completion) can still fail to reach an accepting configuration within a finite token budget, especially under tokenizer-grammar mismatch, because local feasibility ignores whether the remaining budget is actually sufficient to reach acceptance.
payload.method_summary: SWYB (Stay Within Your Bounds) models the grammar as a pushdown automaton (PDA) and offline computes bounded pushdown summaries giving reachability labels and upper-bound distances-to-acceptance for PDA configurations up to a stack-height bound H. Online, these distance estimates drive horizon-aware pruning (discard continuations whose estimated completion cost exceeds the remaining token budget) and a beam search (Distance-Guided Scoring) that rewards tokens making measurable structural progress toward acceptance, guaranteeing every emitted sequence is grammar-accepted.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes SWYB, a lookahead-guided decoding framework for context-free grammars that augments local prefix-feasibility checks with bounded pushdown-automaton distance-to-acceptance estimates, enabling budget-aware pruning and beam search. Across JSON, SQL, and Linear Temporal Logic generation tasks and three base LLMs, SWYB is the only method that achieves 100% syntactic validity in every setting while also improving task-specific accuracy (schema validity, SQL execution accuracy, LTL semantic correctness) over prior constrained decoders, at a moderate decoding-time overhead.
key_architecture_choices: Grammar compiled to a pushdown automaton (PDA); CFG-to-PDA construction is linear in grammar size
Offline-computed bounded pushdown summaries (stack-height bound H, exploration budget B) giving reachability + upper-bound distance-to-acceptance per configuration
Online horizon-aware pruning: discard token continuations whose estimated remaining distance exceeds the remaining token budget
Beam search (Distance-Guided Scoring) that softly promotes tokens making measurable progress toward an accepting configuration
datasets: LTL drone-planning dataset (6,185 examples, from Pan et al. 2023)
payload.headline_results: SWYB achieves 100% syntactic correctness in every domain/model combination (JSON, SQL, LTL across Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-7B), and on Spider it reaches the highest execution accuracy in every setting (e.g. beam-width-4 SWYB improves execution accuracy over GenLM/SynCode baselines) while other constrained decoders (SynCode, XGrammar, GenLM) either miss schema validity or underperform on execution/task accuracy at the same T=120 token budget.
claimed_advantages: Only method achieving 100% syntactic correctness across all three domains and all three base models
Fixes the 'myopia' failure mode of local-feasibility decoders that keep opening nested structures without global lookahead to close them, even with a 40x larger token budget
Soundness holds even with a minimal exploration budget B=1, given a sufficiently large stack-height bound H
Grammar preprocessing (PDA construction + summary) is grammar-dependent, not dataset-dependent, so it is reused across all inputs of a task
limitations: Requires choosing a stack-height bound H and exploration budget B; if H is too low, distances must sometimes be computed online (slower than lookup)
The distance estimate is only an upper bound: a small value certifies a completion exists, but a large value does not prove none exists
Does not incorporate semantic/domain-specific constraints, only syntactic (grammar) validity
Summary precomputation cost can be significant for complex grammars (e.g. 3h40min for SQL with H=13)
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Directly transferable to our hex-meshing DSL decoder's structural-validity problem: our DSL (block/sweep/projection commands with a closed coordinate vocabulary) is plausibly expressible as a context-free grammar, so compiling it to a PDA and using SWYB's offline bounded-distance-to-acceptance summaries plus online horizon-aware pruning/beam search could guarantee every generated program is syntactically well-formed (compiles) within budget, directly addressing care area #1 (structural validity, beam search over program prefixes) and reducing reliance on best-of-N rejection sampling purely for syntax. This is a strong, released-code (github.com/Enzossssss/SWYB), mechanism-level fit even though the evaluated domains (JSON/SQL/LTL) are unrelated to CAD.
payload.reviewer_notes: SWYB only guarantees *grammar* (syntactic) validity, not semantic/geometric validity (e.g. it would not by itself guarantee zero inverted elements or Jacobian quality bounds) — our frozen machine-checkable verifier would still be needed downstream for those checks. Also note our DSL likely has context-sensitive constraints (e.g., referencing specific input-graph face indices via pointer/copy heads) that a plain CFG may not capture; adapting SWYB's PDA formalism to a pointer-augmented grammar would need care. Code is released, which lowers integration cost.
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: M (grammar/PDA construction for our DSL plus offline summary precomputation; runtime beam search integrates with standard autoregressive decoding)

provenance.problem_addressed: Yet, under tokenizer-grammar mismatch and finite token budgets, feasible prefixes may still fail to reach acceptance.
provenance.method_summary: Offline, we compute bounded pushdown summaries with reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, these estimates guide horizon-aware pruning and beam search.
provenance.headline_results: SWYB is the only method that achieves 100% syntactic correctness in every setting.
provenance.limitations: Among the limitations are the stack height bound H and the exploration budget B.

payload.problem_addressed: Long-horizon LLM agent RL trained from sparse, programmatically-verifiable terminal rewards broadcasts one outcome signal to every action in a trajectory (or relies on auxiliary rollout-side signals), discarding the internal structure of the verifier that actually judged success/failure, which limits fine-grained credit assignment.
payload.method_summary: VICT (Verifier-Instrumented Credit Tracing) exposes the terminal verifier's internal checks as executable/evidence-backed 'atoms' with dependency-valid proof edges to actions. Using counterfactual verifier-assignment edits (not new rollouts), it finds a compact dependency-closed 'core' of atoms whose removal/repair would change the verifier's outcome, then redistributes group-relative advantage only along the observed proof edges connecting actions to core atoms; it abstains when evidence is incomplete or ambiguous, changes only the training-time advantage tensor, and requires no learned critic, process labels, or extra rollouts.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces VICT, a training-time interface for long-horizon LLM agent RL that traces a task's terminal verifier's own internal structure back to individual actions through dependency-valid proof edges, and redistributes RL advantage along those edges instead of broadcasting a single sparse outcome. On ALFWorld, WebShop, and tau-bench, VICT substantially outperforms outcome-only GRPO/RLOO and several fine-grained-credit baselines (GiGPO, SALT, HCAPO), is compatible with (and improves on top of) those rollout-side methods, and its verifier-interface diagnostics (reconstruction/mutation conformance, eligibility-invariant pass rate) confirm the credit signal is verifier-backed rather than heuristic.
key_architecture_choices: Verifier exposed as executable/evidence-backed atoms with dependency-valid proof edges to actions, rather than a single scalar reward
Counterfactual verifier-assignment edits (not additional environment rollouts) used to find success/correction cores
Budgeted greedy search for a compact, dependency-closed core of atoms meeting a displacement threshold; abstains if no valid core is found

Core-atom advantage normalized within the same-task rollout group and combined with the base outcome advantage via a clipped, weighted correction (Eq. 9-10), composable with rollout-side credit methods
metrics: WebShop normalized score and strict success rate
verifier-interface diagnostics: reconstruction/mutation conformance, eligibility-invariant pass rate, proof coverage, abstention rate
payload.headline_results: With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VICT improves over GRPO by 18.2 points on ALFWorld average success and 24.9 points on WebShop strict success; with Qwen2.5-7B it reaches 93.7% ALFWorld average / 83.6% WebShop strict success (gains of 16.1/17.5 points over GRPO), and composing VICT with rollout-side methods (GiGPO, SALT, HCAPO) improves over each alone; on tau-bench VICT reaches 56.6/45.1 Retail/Airline pass@1 vs 51.3/40.0 for Fission-GRPO.
claimed_advantages: Uses the verifier's own internal task structure for credit assignment instead of treating it as an opaque scalar
Preserves the original outcome reward; adds no learned critic, process labels, or extra rollouts
Auditable: every non-zero correction is logged with its action, atom, witness, and evidence source
Composable with existing rollout-side fine-grained-credit methods, improving on top of them
limitations: Only applicable where terminal rewards come from verifiers exposable as executable/evidence-backed atoms with observable state changes in trajectory logs; less direct for holistic learned judges or hidden verifier state
Verifier instrumentation has real engineering cost (adapter LoC, person-hours) that grows with instrumentation level
Depends on small, dependency-closed verifier cores; large/ambiguous atom sets can force larger cores or abstention, reducing credit recall
Proof edges certify verifier-defined eligibility, not causal necessity; not a policy-invariant shaping guarantee
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Our frozen, machine-checkable verifier (compiles, zero inverted elements, Jacobian/aspect-ratio bounds, boundary fidelity, feature-edge capture, element-budget) already resembles VICT's target setting: a terminal, programmatically-verifiable check with decomposable sub-checks (per-command/per-face contributions to inverted elements, boundary-fidelity misses, etc.). VICT's approach of tracing which sub-checks each generated command/face-pointer action is responsible for, and shaping RL/best-of-N training advantage accordingly rather than a single pass/fail signal, is directly applicable to strengthening our verifier-in-the-loop training beyond simple rejection sampling — e.g. giving credit/blame to specific block/sweep/projection commands for specific verifier failures (inverted element at a specific hex, surface-fidelity miss at a specific face) instead of only screening whole candidate programs.
payload.reviewer_notes: Evaluated only on text/embodied-agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, tau-bench) with LLM policies, not on any geometric/program-synthesis-for-CAD domain, so the concrete atom/proof-edge instrumentation would need to be redesigned for our mesher's verifier (e.g. treating per-element Jacobian violations or per-face boundary-fidelity misses as atoms). The method assumes the verifier can be instrumented to expose intermediate atoms/dependencies, which is plausible for our deterministic mesher+verifier pipeline but is nontrivial engineering.
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: L (requires instrumenting our verifier to expose atomic checks and dependency/proof edges back to generated commands, not just a pass/fail signal)
dependencies_on_other_methods: Base group-relative RL optimizer (e.g. GRPO/RLOO) whose advantage tensor VICT corrects

provenance.problem_addressed: Standard objectives often train from programmatically verifiable terminal rewards by broadcasting each sparse outcome to every action in a trajectory.
provenance.method_summary: VICT ... exposes executable or evidence backed atoms and traces them back to actions through dependency-valid proof edges.
provenance.headline_results: VICT improves over GRPO by 18.2 points on ALFWorld average success and 24.9 points on WebShop strict success
provenance.limitations: VICT is limited to settings where terminal rewards come from verifiers that can be exposed as executable or evidence-backed atoms

payload.problem_addressed: Digital-twin/world-model-generated synthetic data augments scarce real training data, but the sim-to-real gap means augmentation can fail to improve true population-level performance; practitioners need a statistically valid way to decide, using as few real test points as possible, whether a specific candidate synthetic dataset actually helps.
payload.method_summary: The paper frames the decision as a sequential hypothesis test on the paired loss difference between a model trained on real data alone versus real+synthetic data. Under a symmetry-based null (no distributional shift induced by the synthetic augmentation), it introduces the adaptive e-process sign-flip test (aeSFT), which adaptively grows both the number of Monte Carlo sign-flip resampling rounds (intra-batch e-process) and the amount of real test data consumed (inter-batch e-process), stopping once accumulated evidence exceeds 1/alpha, giving anytime-valid Type-I error control without pre-specifying the test-set size.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes aeSFT, a doubly-adaptive statistical test that decides whether augmenting a real training dataset with a candidate synthetic dataset improves true population-level model performance, using as little real test data as possible while providing anytime-valid Type-I error control. Compared to a fixed-sample sign-flip test, a paired t-test, and an existing adaptive martingale test (aMT), aeSFT detects useful synthetic datasets with substantially fewer real test samples across a synthetic binary-classification task, a digital-twin-aided wireless packet-scheduling task, and a radio-map prediction task, while keeping the false-positive rate below the target level.
key_architecture_choices: Two test formulations: a direct test on the mean paired loss difference, and a symmetry-based sign-flip test with a weaker null assumption for faster evidence accumulation
Doubly-adaptive design: adapts both the number of Monte Carlo sign-flip rounds (compute cost) and the amount of real test data consumed
Intra-batch e-process measures evidence within the current batch; inter-batch e-process compounds evidence across batches
Anytime-valid stopping rule: reject once accumulated evidence exceeds 1/alpha, with no need to pre-specify test-set size
datasets: Synthetic 5-D binary classification task (real vs. covariance/label-perturbed synthetic distribution)
Digital-twin-aided wireless packet-scheduling task (real vs. perturbed-arrival-rate/deadline DT environment)
Sionna-RT radio-map prediction task (high-fidelity real ray-tracing maps vs. 196 lower-fidelity synthetic settings)
metrics: true-positive rate (TPR) / false-positive rate (FPR) vs. consumed real test data
Type-I error control at target level alpha
payload.headline_results: Across all three tasks aeSFT reaches a given TPR with markedly fewer real test samples than the aMT baseline (e.g., in packet scheduling aeSFT hits TPR 0.657 after 16 real episodes vs. near-zero for aMT, and mean stopping time 88.0 vs 143.6 episodes; in radio-map prediction aeSFT identifies 57/123 useful synthetic datasets after just the initial 50-map batch vs. 4/123 for aMT after the full 400-map budget), while its empirical FPR stays below the target alpha=0.1 in every experiment.
claimed_advantages: Anytime-valid: Type-I error controlled without pre-specifying the test-set size, avoiding p-hacking from post-hoc budget increases
Substantially more sample-efficient (fewer real test points) than fixed-sample sign-flip/t-tests and the adaptive martingale baseline (aMT)
Symmetry-based null requires no known finite loss bound (unlike aMT), broadening applicability
General-purpose: applicable to any setting with a paired real-data loss difference, including LLM synthetic-data evaluation, robotics/AV world-model data, and wireless network digital twins
limitations: Symmetry-based test controls Type-I error under a different (stronger) null assumption than the direct mean-based test
Adaptive batch design means TPR curve is necessarily stepwise before the initial batch is consumed
Not evaluated on real production-scale ML systems or on geometric/CAD data; experiments are on small synthetic and simulated engineering tasks
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Directly applicable to our data-diversity/data-volume and domain-gap concern: we train on a mix of inverse-factory-synthesized (B-rep, program) pairs and real, auto-labeled CAD parts, and aeSFT gives a principled, sample-efficient statistical test — using a limited held-out set of real CAD parts — for whether adding more inverse-factory synthetic data (or a proposed new synthetic-generation recipe) actually improves true performance on real parts, rather than just improving on synthetic-distribution validation metrics. This could replace ad-hoc A/B comparisons when deciding whether to scale up the inverse factory vs. invest in more real auto-labeled data, and could also be applied per-subpopulation (e.g. per CAD part family) to detect where synthetic data specifically fails to transfer.
payload.reviewer_notes: The method itself is domain-agnostic statistics (sequential/e-process hypothesis testing) demonstrated on toy/engineering tasks, not on generative CAD/mesh models; applying it to hexgen would require defining an appropriate bounded per-part loss (e.g. verifier pass/fail or hex-quality score) and a limited pool of real, verifier-scored CAD parts held out purely for this test. No code link found in the excerpted text.
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: S-M (mostly a statistical testing procedure to implement/adapt around our existing verifier-derived per-part loss; no model architecture changes needed)

provenance.problem_addressed: Owing to the inevitable simulation-to-reality (sim-to-real) gap, however, augmentation may fail to improve the performance of the trained model on the real data distribution.
provenance.method_summary: we introduce the adaptive e-process sign-flip test (aeSFT), a doubly adaptive procedure that adapts both the number of Monte Carlo sign-flip rounds ... and the amount of real test data consumed.
provenance.headline_results: aeSFT identifies 57 of the 123 useful synthetic datasets after consuming the initial batch of 50 maps.
provenance.limitations: aMT controls Type-I error under the direct mean null H0, whereas SFT, eSFT, and aeSFT control it under the symmetry null H0syn.

payload.problem_addressed: Diffusion-based e-commerce creative generation produces flattened raster images with distorted text/inconsistent product details that need manual refinement, are hard to edit/reuse, and offer no explicit structure to encode complex design requirements as verifiable training signals.
payload.method_summary: CommerceVibe formulates e-commerce creative generation as conditional program synthesis: given product images, a design request, and product info, a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B model autoregressively generates an executable HTML/CSS document. It is trained with SFT on ~28k curated examples, then dual-feedback GRPO reinforcement learning combining (1) a rule-based reward from rendered-document checks (Text/Product/Layout errors, plus critical-error safeguards for overflow, overlap, out-of-canvas elements, occlusion) and (2) a VLM-judge preference reward (Qwen3-VL-Plus scoring 6 visual/commercial dimensions from a rendered screenshot), combined with equal weight into within-group standardized GRPO advantages.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper presents CommerceVibe, which casts e-commerce creative design as generating executable HTML/CSS program output rather than raster pixels, making the result renderable, editable, and reusable and enabling explicit rule-based structural verification. It introduces a dual-feedback reinforcement learning recipe (rule-based structural checks plus VLM-based preference judging) applied via GRPO on top of an SFT policy, and shows on a 1,300-case benchmark (with independent expert evaluation) that this combination outperforms strong external multimodal models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash) as well as SFT-only and single-feedback RL variants.
key_architecture_choices: Output represented as executable HTML/CSS program (conditional program synthesis) rather than raster pixels
Rule-based reward from deterministic checks on the rendered document (Text/Product/Layout error families) plus critical-error safeguard penalties (overflow, overlap, out-of-canvas, occlusion)

VLM-judge preference reward: fixed Qwen3-VL-Plus rates 6 dimensions (visual appeal, product presentation, readability, marketing relevance, commercial usability, copy faithfulness) from a rendered screenshot
Dual-feedback combined with equal weights into standardized within-group GRPO advantages, on top of an SFT-initialized Qwen3.5-9B policy
datasets: 28,568 SFT training examples / 3,174 validation examples of real e-commerce product images + design requests + reference HTML/CSS
1,300-case benchmark (1,140 single-image, 160 multi-image) across 34 e-commerce categories
metrics: Spearman correlation between automatic and expert scores
payload.headline_results: Rule+Preference RL (CommerceVibe) reaches S_overall=94.0 and S_expert=90.0, beating the SFT-only policy (87.3/81.6), single-feedback RL variants, and external models GPT-5.5 (80.1/78.9), Claude Opus 4.8 (77.7/78.4), and Gemini 3.5 Flash (75.3/75.9); ablating any of the three rule families (Text/Product/Layout) degrades its intended dimension, with Layout-rule removal causing the largest drop.
claimed_advantages: Executable-program output enables scalable production, direct editing, and structural/rule-based verification unavailable to raster diffusion outputs
Rule-based and VLM-preference feedback are complementary: combining them gives the largest gains, especially on harder Multi-image cases (+4.8 pts vs best single-feedback variant)
Outperforms strong general-purpose multimodal external models on both automatic and blind expert evaluation
High expert inter-rater agreement (ICC(A,5)=0.811) supporting the validity of automatic scores
limitations: No iterative self-correction/refinement loop yet (single-shot generation without candidate reranking); left as future work (closed-loop self-improvement)
VLM judge (Qwen3-VL-Plus) is fixed and could itself carry biases not audited against multiple independent judges
Domain is e-commerce creative design in HTML/CSS, not evaluated on any geometric/CAD or 3D program-synthesis task
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Strong structural analogy to hexgen: CommerceVibe generates an executable *program* (HTML/CSS) conditioned on multimodal input, verified with deterministic rule-based structural checks (analogous to our compiles/zero-inverted-elements/Jacobian/boundary-fidelity verifier) plus a learned quality judge, and trained via GRPO with within-group standardized advantages on top of SFT — essentially rejection-sampled/RL self-improvement against a verifier, matching our care area #6 (self-play/verifier-in-the-loop training) and #1 (structural validity via verifier-guided generation). The dual-feedback design (hard rule reward + soft learned-quality reward, equally weighted into GRPO advantage) is a directly transferable recipe for combining our frozen machine-checkable mesh verifier with a softer learned quality signal (e.g. a learned mesh-quality critic) during RL fine-tuning of the hexgen decoder, beyond pure best-of-N screening.
payload.reviewer_notes: The 'rule-based' checks here are simple, cheap, differentiable-adjacent structural detectors (text overflow/overlap, out-of-canvas, occlusion) computed directly from the rendered artifact, much cheaper to evaluate per-sample than a full deterministic mesher+verifier pass; this asymmetry (cheap partial checks vs. our expensive full mesh generation+verification) should be kept in mind when adapting the GRPO recipe — sample efficiency of K=8 rollouts per input may not be affordable for us without a cheaper proxy verifier for shaping.
